Verify rewrite DATA ONLY. Do not write improved examples or solve the user's task.
Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

[{"id": "arka-english-main-0-prompt-long-0006", "row_sha256": "2173d380cf26be8db8e7ceddfa0ef55ed120f52c6bedbbbf9621224e46383472", "mode": "/prompt", "language": "en", "context": {}, "identity": false, "mode_instructions": "Organize the supplied request into a clear prompt. Preserve scope and constraints. Do not invent context, requirements, or missing information. Do not perform the task.", "input": "
could you turn this into a clear prompt for an in-product help article about the quiet collection preference in the fictional browser extension folio ferry. i have bits of the setup and the reason people ask about it, but they’re all mixed together. the article should explain what the preference does in plain language for someone who has just opened the extension, not sound like a launch announcement or a technical policy. folio ferry has a narrow sidebar with three places people use a lot: Current tab, Reading shelf, and Activity. Settings is opened from the small gear at the bottom of that sidebar, and inside Settings there is a Sharing section. Quiet collection is listed in that section. please keep those labels as written because they match what appears in the interface.

the preference is called Quiet collection, with both words capitalized like that. It is off by default, and each browser profile has its own setting. switching it on changes where a person’s saved pages go: instead of being sent to the connected workspace, they go to that person’s private Reading shelf. explain that as the central behavior, without suggesting it changes every other sharing control in the extension. a person can turn it off again from the same setting, and after that saved pages go to the connected workspace as they did before. don’t make up an automatic timer, a confirmation screen, or a rule that turns it off when the browser closes, because i haven’t specified any of those things.

there’s one important content restriction i want stated directly: do not publish photos. that wording is important, and it is about publishing photos, not about whether someone can save a page for themselves. the preference should not be presented as a way to publish photos privately, and please don’t stretch the line into a claim that every kind of page or every kind of link is prohibited from being shared. people still need to understand that saving a link is an ordinary allowed action. when Quiet collection is on, a person can save a link to the private Reading shelf. if the preference is off, the saved page goes to the connected workspace under the usual behavior. avoid mixing up saving a page with publishing its photos.

for a simple example, use a person who is looking at a recipe page in the Current tab. they want to keep the page to read later, but don’t want to send it to the connected workspace right now. with Quiet collection turned on, they can save its link to their private Reading shelf. the example should not claim that the extension copies the recipe, downloads its images, or changes the page itself. the person has not asked to publish anything. i want the difference between keeping a link and publishing photos to be easy to follow even for someone who doesn’t know the extension yet.

it may help to mention a short line from a user, something like “I just want to keep this for later.” treat that as an ordinary comment from a person trying the feature, not as a formal slogan and not as a promise about privacy beyond the behavior i described. explain that the person can use the gear, open Settings, choose Sharing, and switch on Quiet collection. then explain where saved pages go. don’t imply they need to sign in again, ask an administrator, or change a workspace setting; none of that is part of this setup.

please make the help article easy to scan. one numbered section would fit naturally for the steps to find and switch the preference on, and the rest can be short connected sections rather than a long list of every possible case. cover what the preference does, how to find it, what happens when it is on, and what returning it to off means. keep the distinction between a browser profile’s setting and the connected workspace understandable, but don’t invent a team role or a way to share the preference across profiles. the activity panel exists in the sidebar, but i don’t know that it needs to be described as part of the setting, so don’t assign it a behavior.

please use a calm, practical tone, like help text someone can read while using Folio Ferry. keep the product and interface names consistent. don’t describe this as a new feature, don’t add a release date, and don’t claim that the setting guarantees anything beyond sending saved pages to the private Reading shelf instead of the connected workspace while it is on. the article should leave the reader with a clear understanding that they can still save links for themselves, and should state the photo restriction plainly. the fact that Quiet collection starts off is useful context, and so is the option to switch it back off from the same place.

one more detail for the ending: the help text should tell the reader where to return if they want to change the preference later, namely Settings, then Sharing, then Quiet collection. keep that as distinct practical information at the end rather than adding a summary slogan. don’t suggest that turning the setting off republishes anything that was saved earlier; there’s no information here about what happens to earlier saved pages. the requested piece is just a help article explaining the stated preference and its ordinary use, not a redesign of the extension or a proposal for extra controls.", "output": "Write an in-product help article explaining the Quiet collection preference in the fictional browser extension Folio Ferry. Use plain, calm, practical language for someone who has just opened the extension. Make the article easy to scan, with short connected sections and one numbered section for the steps to find and switch on the preference. Do not write a launch announcement or a technical policy.

### Interface and preference

Folio Ferry has a narrow sidebar with three commonly used places: Current tab, Reading shelf, and Activity. The small gear at the bottom of the sidebar opens Settings. Quiet collection is listed under the Sharing section in Settings. Keep these interface labels exactly as written.

Quiet collection is off by default, and each browser profile has its own setting. When it is on, saved pages go to the person’s private Reading shelf instead of the connected workspace. When it is off, saved pages go to the connected workspace as they did before. A person can change the preference from the same setting. Explain this central behavior without suggesting that it changes other sharing controls.

### Finding and using Quiet collection

Give clear steps for opening the gear, choosing Settings, opening Sharing, and switching on Quiet collection. Explain where saved pages go while the preference is on, and that the person can return to the same setting to switch it off again. Do not assign a behavior to the Activity panel.

Use a recipe page in Current tab as a simple example: someone wants to keep the page to read later without sending it to the connected workspace right now. With Quiet collection on, they can save its link to their private Reading shelf. Make clear that saving a link is an ordinary allowed action. Do not claim that Folio Ferry copies the recipe, downloads its images, or changes the page.

Include the user’s ordinary comment: “I just want to keep this for later.” Present it as a person’s comment, not a slogan or a promise about privacy beyond the described behavior.

### Photo restriction and scope

State this restriction plainly and exactly: do not publish photos. It concerns publishing photos, not saving a page for oneself. Do not present Quiet collection as a way to publish photos privately, or claim that every kind of page or link is prohibited from being shared. Keep the distinction between saving a link and publishing photos clear.

Explain the difference between a browser profile’s setting and the connected workspace without inventing a team role or a way to share the preference across profiles. Do not add a sign-in step, administrator approval, or workspace setting.

### Closing information

End with the practical location for changing the preference later: Settings, then Sharing, then Quiet collection. Keep this separate from the explanation of what the preference does. Do not add a summary slogan or suggest that switching the setting off republishes pages saved earlier; what happens to earlier saved pages is unspecified.

Do not add an automatic timer, confirmation screen, browser-close rule, release date, or claims that the setting guarantees anything beyond sending saved pages to the private Reading shelf instead of the connected workspace while it is on. Explain only the stated preference and its ordinary use."}]
